The transaction was not designed to advance Cascade\'s interests; it was designed to advance the interests of Whitmore Capital Partners\' broader fund management enterprise by enhancing the value and performance of a different fund\'s portfolio company. This constitutes a waste of corporate assets under Delaware law, and Claimants are entitled to relief accordingly.

**[VII. DAMAGES]{.underline}**

**A. Compensatory Damages Calculation**

Claimants seek compensatory damages representing the value diverted from Cascade through the below-market license of ThermalCore technology to Volaris Manufacturing Group LLC. The compensatory damages calculation is straightforward:

  -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Component**                                                                    **Amount**
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------
  Annual fair market value of ThermalCore license (per Ridgeline Advisory Group)   \$9,500,000

  Annual license fee under the License Agreement                                   \$2,800,000

  Annual damages (differential)                                                    \$6,700,000

  License term                                                                     7 years (March 1, 2023 -- February 28, 2030)

  **Total compensatory damages**                                                   **\$46,900,000**
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

As of the date of this filing (March 15, 2024), the License Agreement has been in effect for approximately 12.5 months. Damages accrued from March 1, 2023 through March 15, 2024 total approximately \$6,979,167 on a prorated basis. Future damages for the remaining approximately 5.95 years of the license term (March 15, 2024 through February 28, 2030) total approximately \$39,865,000, subject to present-value discount at an appropriate rate to be determined at the evidentiary hearing.

These damages represent value diverted from Cascade to Volaris Manufacturing Group LLC, and through Volaris to Whitmore Fund II LP, as a direct result of the below-market license imposed by Whitmore Capital Partners LLC through its control of Cascade\'s Board.

**B. Equitable Relief --- Rescission**

Claimants seek rescission of the Technology License Agreement dated March 1, 2023, between Cascade Thermal Systems Inc. and Volaris Manufacturing Group LLC, in its entirety. The License Agreement was the product of self-dealing by a controlling shareholder, was not approved through the affiliate-transaction procedures required by Section 8.7 of the Operating Agreement, and was executed on terms far below fair market value. The License Agreement was neither fairly negotiated nor fairly priced.

Rescission would restore the status quo ante and prevent ongoing harm to Cascade and its minority shareholders. Upon rescission, Volaris would be required to cease all use of ThermalCore technology, and Cascade would be free to license the technology to any party --- including Volaris, if it so chose --- on arm\'s-length terms reflecting fair market value. Rescission is the most complete remedy for the harm inflicted and is warranted by the circumstances.

**C. Disgorgement of Profits**

In the alternative or in addition to compensatory damages, Claimants seek disgorgement of all profits earned by Volaris Manufacturing Group LLC attributable to its use of ThermalCore technology under the License Agreement. Disgorgement is an appropriate equitable remedy for a controlling shareholder\'s breach of fiduciary duty, particularly where the controlling shareholder\'s affiliate has profited directly from the wrongful conduct. The principle underlying disgorgement is that a fiduciary who profits from a breach of duty should not be permitted to retain the fruits of its wrongdoing.

Claimants reserve the right to present expert testimony at the evidentiary hearing quantifying Volaris\'s profits attributable to the licensed technology. The disgorgement amount may exceed the compensatory damages figure of \$46.9 million to the extent that Volaris\'s profits from exploiting ThermalCore technology exceed the license fee differential.

**D. Attorneys\' Fees and Costs**

Claimants seek an award of reasonable attorneys\' fees, costs, and expenses incurred in prosecuting this arbitration. Under Delaware law, a successful derivative claim may support an award of fees to the derivative plaintiffs\' counsel where the litigation confers a benefit on the corporation. *See, e.g., Sugarland Industries, Inc. v. Thomas*, 420 A.2d 142 (Del. 1980). In addition, Claimants seek reimbursement of the costs incurred in retaining Ridgeline Advisory Group to perform the independent valuation of the ThermalCore technology license, the amount of which will be proved at the evidentiary hearing. Claimants further request that all arbitration costs, including the arbitrator\'s fees and AAA administrative fees, be allocated to Respondent.

It is reasonable to infer that a professional and possibly personal relationship exists between Dr. Alan Fairhaven and Dr. Peshkov arising from this research collaboration. The September 2022 publication date indicates that the research and writing process likely began well before that date, and the professional relationship may have continued beyond publication.

The arbitrator\'s disclosure statement identifies Dr. Alan Fairhaven as her husband and states his former position at the University of Minnesota. The disclosure statement does not reference the co-authored paper, does not identify any relationship between Dr. Alan Fairhaven and Dr. Rita Peshkov, and does not address any connection between the arbitrator\'s spouse and any witness or party representative in this arbitration.

**3.3 Professional Organization Affiliations --- Minnesota ADR Ethics Institute**

The arbitrator has disclosed in her June 17, 2024 disclosure statement that she has served on the **advisory board** of the Minnesota ADR Ethics Institute since 2021. The advisory board provides substantive guidance on programming, ethics standards, and professional development initiatives for the Institute. The arbitrator\'s disclosure also states that **Ellen Wu**, Senior Partner at Barrow & Thistlewood LLP and head of that firm\'s national arbitration practice, also serves on the advisory board of the Minnesota ADR Ethics Institute. The disclosure of Ms. Wu\'s advisory board service was noted in the context of the arbitrator\'s description of her professional affiliations.

**Additional Finding --- Garrett T. Whitmore\'s Involvement.** Public records --- specifically, the IRS Form 990 filings of the Minnesota ADR Ethics Institute --- reveal that **Garrett T. Whitmore**, Founder and Managing Partner of Whitmore Capital Partners LLC (the respondent in this arbitration), serves on the **Board of Trustees** of the Minnesota ADR Ethics Institute. As noted in Section 1.1 above, the Board of Trustees is the Institute\'s governing body, responsible for strategic direction, budgetary oversight, and appointments to leadership positions, including appointments to the advisory board. The advisory board, on which the arbitrator sits, provides substantive guidance on programming and ethics standards, and its members are appointed by or serve at the pleasure of the Board of Trustees.

While the Board of Trustees and the advisory board are formally distinct bodies within the Institute\'s governance structure, they serve the same relatively small nonprofit organization. The Institute\'s publicly available bylaws and posted meeting minutes indicate that both bodies attend the Institute\'s annual meetings, and that periodic joint sessions between the Board of Trustees and the advisory board are held to discuss programming priorities and organizational strategy. Given the small size of the organization and the overlapping meeting structures, it is reasonable to infer that the arbitrator and the respondent\'s principal, Garrett T. Whitmore, interact in the context of their shared service to this organization.

The arbitrator\'s disclosure statement does not reference Garrett T. Whitmore\'s role at the Minnesota ADR Ethics Institute. The disclosure identifies the arbitrator\'s own advisory board service and Ellen Wu\'s advisory board service, but does not address whether any party or party principal serves in any capacity with the Institute.

**3.4 Investment and Financial Interests**

The arbitrator\'s June 17, 2024 disclosure statement indicates that her personal investment portfolio is managed by **Northbridge Wealth Advisors**, an investment management firm. The disclosure statement affirmatively states that the arbitrator holds \"no direct equity positions in any party to this arbitration.\" The disclosure does not further describe the composition of her investment portfolio, and it does not address indirect interests, fund-of-funds exposure, or the specific holdings of any pooled investment vehicle in which she may participate.

**Additional Finding --- Northbridge Select Alternatives Fund.** A review of publicly available SEC filings and fund disclosure documents reveals that Northbridge Wealth Advisors manages a fund-of-funds product called the **Northbridge Select Alternatives Fund**. The Northbridge Select Alternatives Fund is a pooled investment vehicle that allocates capital across a diversified portfolio of private equity, venture capital, and alternative investment funds. Per the fund\'s most recent public filing, dated March 2024, the Northbridge Select Alternatives Fund holds a **2.3% limited partner interest in Whitmore Fund II LP**.

As discussed in Section 1.3 above, Whitmore Fund II LP is the Delaware limited partnership that owns **Volaris Manufacturing Group LLC**, the direct beneficiary of the below-market technology license at the center of this arbitration. The economic outcome of this arbitration --- specifically, any award that results in the rescission, renegotiation, or repricing of the Volaris license agreement, or that imposes damages on Whitmore Capital Partners LLC --- has the potential to affect the value of Whitmore Fund II LP\'s portfolio and, by extension, the value of any limited partner interest in Fund II.

If the arbitrator\'s personal investment portfolio, which is managed by Northbridge Wealth Advisors, includes allocations to the Northbridge Select Alternatives Fund --- a product managed by the same firm that manages her portfolio --- she may hold an **indirect financial interest** in Whitmore Fund II LP, and by extension, in the economic outcome of this arbitration. The chain of potential interest is as follows:

> Arbitrator\'s investment portfolio (managed by Northbridge Wealth Advisors)
>
> → Potential allocation to Northbridge Select Alternatives Fund (managed by the same firm)
>
> → Northbridge Select Alternatives Fund holds a 2.3% LP interest in Whitmore Fund II LP
>
> → Whitmore Fund II LP owns Volaris Manufacturing Group LLC
>
> → Volaris is the beneficiary of the disputed \$2.8 million/year technology license (independently valued at \$9.5 million/year FMV)

It must be noted that the publicly available information does not confirm whether the arbitrator\'s personal portfolio includes an allocation to the Northbridge Select Alternatives Fund. However, the fact that her portfolio is managed by the same firm that manages the fund-of-funds product, and that the fund-of-funds product holds a limited partner interest in a fund managed by the respondent, raises a question that warrants further inquiry.

The arbitrator\'s disclosure uses the phrase \"no direct equity positions,\" which would be technically accurate even if she holds an indirect interest through a fund-of-funds structure. A limited partner interest held through a fund-of-funds vehicle is not a \"direct equity position\" in any party; rather, it is an indirect financial exposure layered through two intermediate entities. The arbitrator\'s disclosure does not address indirect interests, does not reference fund-of-funds exposure, and does not identify the specific holdings of the Northbridge Select Alternatives Fund or any other pooled investment vehicle in which she may participate.

**3.5 Arbitration History and Pending Matters Involving Parties\' Counsel**

ewood LLP represented claimant. Judge Fairhaven served as panel chair on a three-arbitrator panel. Award rendered in favor of claimant.

> 4\. *Clearwater Dynamics LLC v. Prism Health Partners* (2023) --- Fielding Marsh & Collier LLP represented claimant. Judge Fairhaven served as sole arbitrator. Award rendered in favor of respondent.
>
> 5\. *Braddock Industries v. Summit Ridge Capital* (2022) --- Barrow & Thistlewood LLP represented claimant. Judge Fairhaven served as co-arbitrator (party-appointed by claimant side). Award rendered in favor of claimant.
>
> 6\. *Orion Fabrication v. Mountain West Supply* (2023) --- Barrow & Thistlewood LLP represents respondent. Judge Fairhaven serves as sole arbitrator. **Matter is currently pending.**
>
> 7\. *DataSync Solutions v. PivotEdge Analytics* (2024) --- Fielding Marsh & Collier LLP represented respondent. Judge Fairhaven served as sole arbitrator. Award rendered in favor of respondent.

The arbitrator\'s disclosure lists only two pending matters in which Barrow & Thistlewood LLP serves as counsel: this case and *Orion Fabrication v. Mountain West Supply*. The omission of *Halcyon Biotech v. Stonewall Partners* from the arbitrator\'s disclosure appears to be either an inadvertent error or a deliberate omission. In either case, the result is that the disclosure understates the number of concurrent pending matters in which the arbitrator and Barrow & Thistlewood LLP are simultaneously engaged.

**Broader Appointment Data (Last 20 Completed Arbitrations, 2021--2024).** A compilation of the arbitrator\'s last 20 completed arbitrations between 2021 and 2024 yields the following data regarding her appointment history with the counsel in this matter:

> • Nine (9) of the 20 completed matters involved Barrow & Thistlewood LLP as counsel for one of the parties, representing **45%** of all completed matters during this period.
>
> • Four (4) of the 20 completed matters involved Fielding Marsh & Collier LLP as counsel for one of the parties, representing **20%** of all completed matters during this period.

**Estimated Fee Data (Past 36 Months).** Based on estimated hourly rates, publicly available matter descriptions, and reasonable assumptions about matter duration, the following fee estimates have been compiled for the arbitrator\'s income from matters involving the parties\' counsel over the past 36 months:

**3.6 CLE and Speaking Engagements**

A review of CLE event archives, including the Lakeview Dispute Resolution Center\'s publicly available event listings and the Minnesota State Bar Association\'s CLE records, reveals the following event relevant to this arbitration.

**October 14, 2023 CLE Event.** The Lakeview Dispute Resolution Center hosted a Continuing Legal Education event titled **\"Arbitrating Complex IP Licensing Disputes\"** on October 14, 2023, at its offices at 750 Nicollet Mall, Suite 3200, Minneapolis, Minnesota 55402. The event was a panel discussion addressing current trends, best practices, and emerging issues in the arbitration of intellectual property licensing disputes, with a focus on valuation methodologies, arbitrator selection in technology-intensive cases, and the management of expert testimony.

The listed panelists for the event were:

> • **Hon. Margaret R. Fairhaven (Ret.)** --- the sole arbitrator in this matter
>
> • **Dominic Hargrave** --- Lead Partner, Barrow & Thistlewood LLP, and lead counsel for Whitmore Capital Partners LLC (the respondent) in this arbitration
>
> • Professor Naomi J. Strickland, University of Minnesota Law School
>
> • Marcus DelVecchio, Partner, Henning & Burwell P.A.

The event occurred on October 14, 2023, approximately **five months** before the arbitration demand was filed on March 15, 2024, and approximately **eight months** before the arbitrator\'s appointment was confirmed on June 10, 2024. The topic of the CLE event --- arbitrating complex IP licensing disputes --- is **directly germane** to the subject matter of this arbitration, which concerns the valuation and enforceability of a technology license for Cascade\'s proprietary ThermalCore heat-exchange technology.

Co-panelist service at a CLE event involves shared preparation, coordination of presentation materials, interaction during the panel discussion, and typically informal professional interaction before and after the event. This type of shared professional activity can give rise to collegial familiarity and a collaborative professional relationship between the co-panelists.

The arbitrator\'s June 17, 2024 disclosure statement does not reference this CLE event, does not identify Judge Fairhaven and Mr. Hargrave as co-panelists, and does not otherwise disclose a professional relationship with Mr. Hargrave beyond the arbitration matters in which Barrow & Thistlewood LLP has appeared as counsel.

**[SECTION IV: THIRD-PARTY ENTITIES]{.underline}**

**4.1 Lakeview Dispute Resolution Center**

The Lakeview Dispute Resolution Center is an alternative dispute resolution provider located at 750 Nicollet Mall, Suite 3200, Minneapolis, Minnesota 55402. The Managing Director of the center is Harold Lund. The arbitrator, Hon. Margaret R. Fairhaven (Ret.), is affiliated with Lakeview as a neutral. The financial terms of the affiliation --- including whether Lakeview takes a percentage of the arbitrator\'s fees for matters administered through the center, whether Lakeview receives separate administrative fees for referred matters, or whether Lakeview\'s revenue model depends on maintaining referral relationships with law firms that regularly retain its affiliated neutrals --- are not publicly available. These financial arrangements may be relevant to evaluating the nature and extent of any economic interdependency between the arbitrator, Lakeview, and the referring law firms.

As discussed in Section III.6 above, Lakeview hosted the October 14, 2023 CLE event titled \"Arbitrating Complex IP Licensing Disputes,\" at which Judge Fairhaven and Mr. Hargrave served as co-panelists.

**4.2 Minnesota ADR Ethics Institute**

The Minnesota ADR Ethics Institute is a nonprofit professional organization focused on promoting ethical standards in alternative dispute resolution. The Institute provides programming, publications, and professional development opportunities for ADR practitioners, attorneys, corporate users of arbitration, and academic researchers in the fields of mediation, arbitration, and related dispute resolution processes.

The Institute\'s governance structure includes two principal bodies: a **Board of Trustees**, which serves as the governing body of the organization, and an **advisory board**, which provides substantive guidance on programming, ethics standards, and professional development initiatives.

The following affiliations with the Minnesota ADR Ethics Institute are relevant to this matter:

> • **Board of Trustees:** Garrett T. Whitmore, Founder and Managing Partner of Whitmore Capital Partners LLC (the respondent in this arbitration) --- per IRS Form 990 filings for fiscal year 2023.
>
> • **Advisory Board:** Hon. Margaret R. Fairhaven (Ret.) (the arbitrator in this matter) --- since 2021, per her disclosure statement.
>
> • **Advisory Board:** Ellen Wu, Senior Partner, Barrow & Thistlewood LLP (head of the firm\'s national arbitration practice; involved in arbitrator selection strategy for this matter) --- per the arbitrator\'s disclosure statement.

The Institute is described in its public materials as a small nonprofit with limited staff and a focused mission centered on ADR ethics. Annual meetings and joint sessions between the Board of Trustees and the advisory board are held to coordinate programming and organizational strategy, per the Institute\'s publicly available bylaws and posted meeting minutes. The small size of the organization and the overlapping meeting structures increase the likelihood of direct personal interaction among members of both bodies.

Cross-references: See Section 1.1 (Garrett T. Whitmore), Section 2.1 (Ellen Wu), and Section III.3 (arbitrator\'s affiliation) above.

**4.3 Northbridge Wealth Advisors**

Northbridge Wealth Advisors is an investment management firm that manages the arbitrator\'s personal investment portfolio, as disclosed in the arbitrator\'s June 17, 2024 disclosure statement. In addition to managing individual client portfolios, Northbridge Wealth Advisors manages the **Northbridge Select Alternatives Fund**, a fund-of-funds product that allocates capital across a diversified portfolio of private equity, venture capital, and alternative investment strategies.

Per the Northbridge Select Alternatives Fund\'s most recent public filing, dated March 2024, the fund holds a **2.3% limited partner interest in Whitmore Fund II LP**. Whitmore Fund II LP is a Delaware limited partnership managed by Whitmore Capital Partners LLC (the respondent in this arbitration) and is the fund that owns Volaris Manufacturing Group LLC, the direct beneficiary of the disputed ThermalCore technology license. The potential chain of indirect financial interest between the arbitrator and Whitmore Fund II LP, through the Northbridge Select Alternatives Fund, is discussed in detail in Section III.4 above.

**4.4 Ridgeline Advisory Group**

Ridgeline Advisory Group is an independent valuation firm that prepared the fair market value assessment of the ThermalCore technology license at issue in this arbitration. N("**Most of the undisclosed facts point toward Respondent, not Claimant.** Seven of the eight omitted matters, the Institute/Whitmore connection, the Northbridge/Fund II exposure, and the CLE with you all bear on her relationship with our side. Correctly computed, matters involving this firm generated **$1,020,000 of $1,974,000 (51.7%)** of her fee income across the 20 completed matters in the workbook, and our clients prevailed in **8 of 9 (88.9%)** of them — not the 48.0% and 7 of 9 reported in the workbook summary and the June 19 memo.")
N("**If Cascade learns these facts, a challenge would very likely succeed** under the R-16/R-17 “justifiable doubt” standard, and — critically — R-18(f) would **not** treat Cascade as having waived grounds that were not and could not reasonably have been known. Cascade could therefore challenge mid-proceeding (forcing replacement and possible repetition under R-19) or, worse, move to vacate a favorable award for “evident partiality” under FAA § 10(a)(2). Every one of the Respondent-side facts is already within our client’s or this firm’s knowledge, so Whitmore cannot plausibly claim surprise, and any later revelation that we sat on them would be damaging to the award and to the firm.")
N("**Whitmore has its own non-frivolous ground** — the spouse/Peshkov co-authorship — and it is the one ground that Whitmore can waive by silence. Because Whitmore (and this firm) now know of it, R-18(f) waiver will attach if no written challenge or reservation is made by June 24.")
P("**Recommendation:** Do not stay silent. Before June 24, file with the AAA (copying Fielding Marsh; no ex parte contact with the arbitrator, R-20) a written request under R-17(b)–(d) that the arbitrator supplement her disclosure on each of the items listed in Section VIII, coupled with an express, protective objection/reservation on the spouse–Peshkov ground so that Whitmore’s right is not waived. This (a) protects any eventual award by putting every known circumstance before both parties and triggering Cascade’s seven-day R-18 clock; (b) preserves Whitmore’s own challenge; and (c) avoids any suggestion that this firm concealed circumstances it knew to bear on the arbitrator’s impartiality. Client authorization from Whitmore is required before filing because the request will surface facts unfavorable to its preferred arbitrator (Whitmore ranked her first; Cascade ranked her third). Given Ellen Wu’s personal connection to the arbitrator (shared advisory board service and involvement in selection strategy), we recommend that the decision be made by you and the client without Ms. Wu’s participation.", align="j")

H("II. Background and Procedural Posture")
B("**The dispute.** Cascade’s minority shareholders (38%), led by director Janet Okafor (11.4%), allege that Whitmore, as manager of Fund III (62% owner of Cascade) and Fund II (owner of Volaris), caused Cascade to grant Volaris an exclusive seven-year ThermalCore license at $2.8M/year against a Ridgeline fair market value of $9.5M/year. Claimed compensatory damages are $46.9M ($6.7M × 7), plus rescission and disgorgement. Seat: Minneapolis; Delaware substantive law; FAA governs the arbitration agreement (Operating Agreement § 12.3; sole arbitrator).")
B("**Witnesses identified in the Demand.** Fact: Janet Okafor; Garrett T. Whitmore (adverse); Thomas Kinnear (Volaris CEO); other Cascade directors. Expert: Ridgeline valuation expert; **Dr. Rita Peshkov** (Cascade VP R&D, named inventor on most of the 14 patents; “key expert witness” on technical value and on the technical basis for Ridgeline’s methodology); a damages expert.")
B("**Selection.** Parties selected Judge Fairhaven on June 3, 2024 (Whitmore ranked her #1; Cascade #3). AAA confirmed on June 10. Disclosure dated June 17. The disclosure states that objections are due June 24, 2024 (seven calendar days after the disclosure). June 24, 2024 is a Monday.")
B("**Arbitrator’s workload with counsel.** The workbook shows 20 completed matters (2021–2024) and five pending matters, three of which (this case, Orion Fabrication, Halcyon Biotech) involve this firm. She reports roughly 85 arbitrations since 2020, so the workbook is a subset — a point to keep in mind when characterizing income dependence (see Section IV.2).")

H("III. Governing Standards")
H("A. AAA Commercial Rules (as excerpted in the record)", 2)
B("**R-16** — disclose “any circumstance likely to give rise to justifiable doubt as to the arbitrator’s impartiality or independence,” including “any past or present relationship with the parties, their representatives, or their counsel”; the obligation is to be “construed broadly,” measured by what “a reasonable person would consider relevant.”")
B("**R-17(a)(i)** — any known “direct or indirect financial or personal interest,” including an interest “in any entity that may be affected by the result of the proceeding.”")
B("**R-17(a)(ii)** — existing or past financial, business, professional, family, or social relationships with any party, counsel, representatives, or **witnesses**, “including, without limitation, relationships arising from … professional association, … board memberships, academic collaboration, or regular social contact.”")
B("**R-17(a)(iii)** — “any prior or pending cases” with any party or its counsel, “whether administered by the AAA or by any other arbitral institution.” This is not limited to matters the arbitrator considers significant.")
B("**R-17(a)(iv)** — catch-all, broadly construed, expressly including “public statements, or expressed views on legal or factual issues relevant to the dispute.”")
B("**R-17(b)–(d)** — continuing duty; arbitrator may not await inquiry; incomplete disclosure may result in removal under R-18 and “may constitute grounds for vacatur … under … 9 U.S.C. § 10”; AAA may request supplemental disclosure before acting on a challenge.")
B("**R-18(a)** — written challenge, “stating with specificity the grounds,” to the AAA and the other party within seven calendar days after the later of (i) communication of the appointment or (ii) when the circumstances “became known or should reasonably have become known.” **R-18(d)** — AAA decides, considering “the disclosures required but not made.” **R-18(f)** — failure to timely challenge waives grounds “then known,” but not grounds that “were not and could not reasonably have been known,” and does not preclude evident-partiality arguments on previously unknown facts at the vacatur stage.")
B("**R-19** — replacement via R-12; replacement arbitrator decides whether prior proceedings are repeated. **R-20** — no ex parte communications; written communications must be shared. **R-48** — challenge notices must be served by means reasonably calculated to ensure timely receipt.")
P("Note: the record contains a compiled set of rule excerpts. Before filing, the rule numbers and text (particularly the R-18 seven-day period) should be confirmed against the official AAA publication.", italic=True)
H("B. Code of Ethics and IBA Guidelines", 2)
B("**AAA/ABA Code of Ethics for Arbitrators in Commercial Disputes (2004), Canon II** — disclosure of known direct or indirect interests and existing or past relationships, including those of family members; a duty to make a **reasonable effort to inform** oneself of such interests and relationships (Canon II.B); doubts resolved in favor of disclosure (Canon II.D); continuing obligation (Canon II.C).")
B("**IBA Guidelines on Conflicts of Interest (2014)** (persuasive only in a domestic AAA case) — General Standard 3(d) (doubts resolved in favor of disclosure) and 7(d) (duty of reasonable enquiry). Relevant lists: Waivable Red List 2.2.1 (direct or indirect shareholding in a privately held party or affiliate); Orange List 3.1.3 (two or more appointments by one party in three years), 3.1.5 (concurrent service in a related matter involving a party), **3.3.8 (appointed more than three times by the same counsel or law firm within three years)**, 3.5.2 (publicly advocated a position on the case). Green List 4.3.1 (shared membership in a professional association with counsel) and 4.3.4 (joint conference speaking with counsel) — relevant to the Ellen Wu and CLE items standing alone.")
H("C. Judicial Review", 2)
P("A court at the seat (D. Minn./Eighth Circuit) may vacate for “evident partiality” under FAA § 10(a)(2). Key authorities to be confirmed and updated before any filing (cited from general knowledge; not included in the record provided): Commonwealth Coatings Corp. v. Continental Casualty Co., 393 U.S. 145 (1968) (vacatur where arbitrator failed to disclose a significant business relationship with a party); Monster Energy Co. v. City Beverages, LLC, 940 F.3d 1130 (9th Cir. 2019) (vacatur where arbitrator failed to disclose ownership interest in the institution and the institution’s repeat business with a party); Applied Industrial Materials Corp. v. Ovalar Makine, 492 F.3d 132 (2d Cir. 2007) (arbitrator aware of a potential conflict must investigate or disclose); Positive Software Solutions, Inc. v. New Century Mortgage Corp., 476 F.3d 278 (5th Cir. 2007) (en banc) (trivial or remote undisclosed relationships insufficient); Halliburton Co. v. Chubb Bermuda Insurance Ltd. [2020] UKSC 48 (persuasive: undisclosed overlapping appointments involving a common party). Minnesota’s Revised Uniform Arbitration Act (Minn. Stat. ch. 572B, incl. §§ 572B.12 and 572B.23) contains a presumption of evident partiality where an arbitrator fails to disclose a known, direct and material interest in the outcome or a known, existing and substantial relationship with a party; its application alongside the FAA should be confirmed.", align="j")
EOF
echo ok'

P("**Assessment.** This is the strongest ground. Under R-18(d) the AAA weighs “disclosures required but not made.” IBA Orange List 3.3.8 (more than three appointments involving the same firm within three years) is satisfied many times over. The omission of Westbrook and Thornwall (Fielding Marsh losses) also undermines any argument that the omissions were neutral.", align="j")

H("2. Economic Dependence and Repeat-Player Concerns", 2)
P("**Corrected figures (workbook Case List, 20 completed matters):**", align="j")
T(["Metric", "Workbook / June 19 memo", "Corrected (recomputed from Case List rows)"], [

 ["FM client prevailed", "1 of 4 (25.0%)", "1 of 4 adjudicated (25.0%) (confirmed) + 1 settled"],
 ["Pending fees involving B&T", "$560,000 of $835,000 (67.1%)", "Confirmed: this matter $340,000 + Orion $45,000 + Halcyon $175,000"],
 ["Completed + pending, B&T share", "—", "$1,580,000 of $2,809,000 (56.2%); excluding this matter, $1,240,000 of $2,469,000 (50.2%)"],
], widths=[1.8, 2.0, 2.7], fs=8.5)
P("**Analysis.** On any computation, roughly half of the arbitrator’s documented fee income over the period derives from matters in which this firm appeared, she has three concurrent matters involving this firm (including one where an award is expected within 60 days), and our clients have prevailed in nearly nine of ten. But the R-16 standard is whether a reasonable person would consider the circumstance relevant, and an income concentration of this magnitude, undisclosed, is the type of economic relationship that Commonwealth Coatings and Monster Energy treat as material. The fees are paid by the parties, not counsel, but the repeat-appointment relationship is with counsel. **Who raises it:** Cascade. **Strength:** High when combined with Issue 1. Caveat: the fee figures are estimates compiled from public data; any filing should describe them as such.", align="j")

Any award or new appointment involving this firm during the pendency of this matter is a continuing-disclosure event under R-17(b) and should be expressly requested.", align="j")

H("3. Garrett T. Whitmore — Board of Trustees, Minnesota ADR Ethics Institute", 2)

The Institute is a small organization.", align="j")
P("**Assessment.** R-17(a)(ii) expressly identifies “board memberships” and “professional association” with a party or witness. Given the small size of the body and joint sessions, it is unlikely she was unaware of his role. **Who raises it:** Cascade. **Strength:** High, and it compounds Issue 8 (Ms. Wu sits on the same advisory board and was involved in selection strategy). H("4. Indirect Financial Interest — Northbridge Select Alternatives Fund / Whitmore Fund II LP", 2)
P("**What the disclosure says.** Section IV: her portfolio is managed on a discretionary basis by Northbridge Wealth Advisors; she holds “no direct equity positions in any party”; she has “not undertaken a position-by-position review” of pooled vehicles or fund-of-funds structures; and she is “not aware” of any material indirect interest.", align="j")

P("**What the record shows.** Dr. Alan Fairhaven and Dr. Rita Peshkov co-authored “Optimization of Phase-Change Heat Exchangers in High-Load Industrial Applications,” Journal of Advanced Thermal Engineering, Vol. 42, Issue 3 (September 2022) — three years after his retirement from teaching. Dr. Peshkov is a Cascade employee (VP R&D since 2017), the named inventor on most ThermalCore patents, and Claimant’s “key expert witness”; the paper’s subject (phase-change heat exchangers for high-load industrial use) is the ThermalCore technology class.", align="j")
P("**Assessment.** R-17(a)(ii) expressly covers past “professional, family” relationships with “witnesses,” and lists “academic collaboration.” The Code of Ethics extends disclosure to family members’ relationships. The disclosure’s qualifiers (“currently,” “any party”) do not cure the omission, and its statement that her husband has no professional relationship with Cascade’s employees appears inaccurate as to a past relationship. The concern is concrete: the arbitrator will assess Dr. Peshkov’s credibility and the uniqueness/value of the technology, which drives the $9.5M FMV and the $46.9M claim; she may also be exposed to her husband’s views on the technology. Mitigating factors: one paper, two years old, no evidence of current collaboration or financial ties; it is the spouse’s, not the arbitrator’s, relationship. **Who raises it:** Whitmore. **Strength:** Moderate–High; stronger if inquiry shows continuing collaboration, joint grants, or any consulting with Cascade. **Waiver:** this is the one ground Whitmore loses by silence (R-18(a)(ii), (f)), because it is now known to us (June 19 memo).", align="j")

H("6. CLE Co-Panel with Dominic Hargrave (October 14, 2023)", 2)
P("**What the record shows.** Judge Fairhaven and you were co-panelists on “Arbitrating Complex IP Licensing Disputes,” hosted by Lakeview at its offices, five months before the Demand. Topics included valuation methodologies, arbitrator selection in technology-intensive cases, and management of expert testimony — all live issues here (Ridgeline’s methodology; Dr. Peshkov’s expert role). Not disclosed.", align="j")
P("**Assessment.** Standing alone, joint conference speaking with counsel is ordinarily non-disqualifying (IBA Green List 4.3.4), so this is not an independent removal ground. But under the broader AAA standard it is a “professional” relationship with lead counsel under R-17(a)(ii) and potentially “expressed views on legal or factual issues relevant to the dispute” under R-17(a)(iv), and it occurred at the institution with which she is affiliated and which receives referrals from this firm. In combination with Issues 1–3, it supports a narrative of a close professional relationship with Respondent’s side. Its omission is hard to explain: she was on the panel, and the Demand names you. **Who raises it:** Cascade. **Strength:** Moderate as an aggravating factor. **Action:** please confirm the nature of your preparation/interaction for the panel, any subsequent contact, and whether any recording or materials exist that reflect her views on valuation or expert evidence.", align="j")

H("7. Lakeview Dispute Resolution Center Affiliation", 2)
P("**What the disclosure says.** Section VII discloses the affiliation and that Lakeview receives referrals from both firms, characterizes this as typical, and notes Lakeview has no role in this AAA case.", align="j")
P("**What is missing.** The structure of her relationship (employee, independent contractor, member/owner), whether she shares in Lakeview revenues or administrative fees, and the volume and value of referrals from each firm. Lakeview also hosted the undisclosed CLE with you.", align="j")
P("**Assessment.** Monster Energy vacated an award where the arbitrator did not disclose an ownership interest in the provider and the provider’s repeat business with a party; if she has an equity or revenue interest in Lakeview and this firm is a material referral source, the same logic applies to counsel. The disclosure’s reassurance that referrals do not influence her is not a substitute for the facts. **Who raises it:** Either party (both firms refer). **Strength:** Moderate pending the facts; potentially High if she has an ownership interest and referrals from this firm are significant.", align="j")

H("8. Ellen Wu — Shared Advisory Board Service", 2)
P("The disclosure accurately discloses Ms. Wu’s advisory board service since 2021, and alone this is a Green List-type association. Two qualifications: (i) the disclosure describes the board’s role as “non-binding guidance,” while the Institute materials describe “substantive guidance on programming, ethics standards, and professional development”; and (ii) Ms. Wu heads this firm’s arbitration practice and was involved in arbitrator selection strategy for this case, which Cascade may characterize as Respondent choosing a familiar colleague. Combined with Issue 3 (Mr. Whitmore on the governing board of the same small organization), the Institute connection links the arbitrator to Respondent’s principal and Respondent’s practice head. **Strength:** Low alone; aggravating in combination.", align="j")

H("9. Subject-Matter Experience and Possible Issue Conflicts", 2)
P("Section VIII states she has presided over “numerous” arbitrations involving technology licensing, IP valuation, and “fiduciary duty claims in the context of private equity portfolio management,” including “the standards of care applicable to investment fund managers in connection with portfolio company transactions.” Expertise is not a conflict, but (i) the statement implies prior rulings on the same legal issues, potentially in matters involving these counsel (e.g., Braddock v. Summit Ridge Capital, an earn-out dispute in which she was this firm’s party-appointed arbitrator; Westbrook Partners v. Arcadian Ventures), which would bear on IBA Orange List 3.1.5 and R-17(a)(iv); and (ii) the CLE and any publications may reflect views on reasonable-royalty and valuation methods. We should request identification (anonymized if confidential) of prior matters addressing PE fund manager duties in cross-fund or affiliate transactions, and any publications or public statements on those issues. **Strength:** Low–Moderate pending responses.", align="j")

H("10. Certification, Timing and Other Defects", 2)
B("**Certification.** Section X certifies completeness “based on a diligent inquiry” while Section IV concedes no position-level review. The certification is contradicted by the record on at least the case list, which is within her own knowledge. R-17(d) makes incomplete disclosure a removal and vacatur ground, and the AAA will view the inaccuracy as aggravating.")
B("**Narrow drafting.** Repeated limiting language — “direct” equity (IV), “currently” and “any party” (V), “socialized with … counsel” (V), “to the best of my recollection” (III) — tracks almost exactly the relationships that were omitted. This pattern will be emphasized by any challenger.")
B("**Confidential-name entry.** Item 3 (Fielding Marsh settled matter, 2021) withholds names; withholding is acceptable but the case number, her role, and counsel on the other side should be provided (the workbook lists the opposing counsel as “Undisclosed”).")
B("**Timing.** R-12(a) contemplates that disclosures accompany the list; here disclosure followed selection (June 3) and confirmation (June 10). Not itself a ground, but it means the parties ranked her without the facts.")
B("**Deadline statement.** The disclosure states the objection period runs seven days from the disclosure (June 24). Under R-18(a) the period runs from the later of communication of the appointment or knowledge of the circumstances. For Whitmore, the facts in the June 19 memo are known now; we should treat June 24 as the outside date for every ground Whitmore might raise. For Cascade, the clock on undisclosed facts will not start until it learns them.")
B("**Items checked and found accurate.** Fee math (400 hours × $850 = $340,000; 15 days × 8 hours = 120 hearing hours; $170,000 per party); hearing window January 13 – February 7, 2025 accommodates 15 hearing days; disclosed matter details (roles, outcomes, counsel) for the seven listed matters are consistent with the workbook; Orion was appointed September 15, 2023 with $45,000 remaining fees.")
EOF

S=/home/user/Lawless_Research_Lab/harvey_lab/sbx.sh; R=/home/user/Lawless_Research_Lab/harvey_lab/vendor/harvey-labs/results/arbitration-international-dispute-resolution/identify-issues-in-arbitrator-disclosure-statement/claude-code-session/20261016-031557; $S $R 'cat > /workspace/build3.py <<"EOF"
H("IV. Issue-by-Issue Analysis")
P("The summary matrix below ranks each issue by the strength of a challenge if raised, and identifies which side the issue favors (i.e., who would raise it). Detailed analysis follows.", align="j")
T(["#", "Issue", "Disclosure section", "Disclosed?", "Rule hook", "Side likely to raise", "Challenge strength"], [
 ["1", "Eight omitted prior/pending matters with counsel (incl. Westbrook head-to-head and pending Halcyon)", "III, X", "No", "R-17(a)(iii); R-18(d)", "Cascade", "High"],
 ["2", "Economic dependence on this firm (51.7% of fees; 8 of 9 wins; 3 concurrent matters)", "III, IX", "No", "R-16; R-17(a)(ii),(iv); IBA 3.3.8", "Cascade", "High (cumulative)"],
 ["3", "Garrett T. Whitmore — Trustee of Institute whose advisory board she serves on", "VI", "No", "R-17(a)(ii) (board memberships)", "Cascade", "High"],
 ["4", "Indirect interest in Whitmore Fund II LP via Northbridge Select Alternatives Fund", "IV", "No (“no direct equity”)", "R-17(a)(i); Canon II.B; IBA 2.2.1", "Cascade", "High if confirmed; inquiry failure regardless"],
 ["5", "Spouse co-authored 2022 paper with Dr. Peshkov on phase-change heat exchangers", "V", "No; affirmative denial", "R-17(a)(ii) (family; academic collaboration; witnesses)", "Whitmore", "Moderate–High"],
 ["6", "CLE co-panel with D. Hargrave (Oct. 14, 2023) on IP licensing arbitration, hosted by Lakeview", "VI, VII, VIII", "No", "R-17(a)(ii),(iv)", "Cascade", "Moderate (aggravating)"],
 ["7", "Lakeview: financial terms, referral volume from both firms", "VII", "Partial", "R-17(a)(i),(ii)", "Either", "Moderate (needs facts)"],
 ["8", "Ellen Wu shared advisory board; Wu’s role in selection", "VI", "Partial", "R-17(a)(ii)", "Cascade", "Low alone; aggravating"],
 ["9", "Subject-matter statements / possible issue conflicts and expressed views", "VIII", "Partial", "R-17(a)(iv); IBA 3.1.5, 3.5.2", "Either", "Low–Moderate"],
 ["10", "Certification of completeness; timing; inaccurate characterizations", "I, X", "—", "R-17(d); Canon II", "Either", "Aggravating"],
], widths=[0.3, 1.9, 0.8, 0.8, 1.1, 0.8, 0.9], fs=8.5)

H("1. Omitted Prior and Pending Matters with Counsel", 2)
P("**What the disclosure says.** Section III lists seven matters (four involving this firm, three involving Fielding Marsh) and states: “To the best of my recollection, the foregoing represents a complete list of arbitrations in which I have served alongside counsel from either Barrow & Thistlewood LLP or Fielding Marsh & Collier LLP.” Section X certifies, “based on a diligent inquiry,” that the statement is complete.", align="j")
P("**What the record shows.** The workbook identifies eight additional matters within R-17(a)(iii) that are not disclosed:", align="j")
T(["Case No.", "Matter (year)", "Firm role", "Outcome for firm’s client", "Est. fee"], [
 ["01-22-0002015", "Crestfield Energy v. Loran Industrial (2022)", "B&T for Claimant", "Won", "$110,000"],
 ["01-22-0002089", "Ashford Medical Devices v. Greenway Therapeutics (2022)", "B&T for Respondent", "Won", "$92,000"],
 ["01-22-0002134", "Westbrook Partners v. Arcadian Ventures (2022)", "FM for Claimant v. B&T for Respondent", "B&T won; FM lost", "$130,000"],
 ["01-23-0002445", "Trident Coatings v. Bayshore Chemical (2023)", "B&T for Claimant", "Lost", "$105,000"],
 ["01-23-0002578", "Redstone Logistics v. Fairfield Transport (2023)", "B&T for Respondent", "Won", "$118,000"],
 ["01-23-0002643", "Thornwall Systems v. Kessler Automation (2023)", "FM for Respondent", "FM lost", "$82,000"],
 ["01-23-0002789", "Warwick Technologies v. Cypress Digital (2023)", "B&T for Claimant", "Won", "$97,000"],
 ["01-24-0003105", "Halcyon Biotech v. Stonewall Partners (appointed Apr. 22, 2024; pending)", "B&T for Respondent", "Pending (pre-hearing)", "$175,000 remaining"],
], widths=[1.0, 2.3, 1.4, 1.1, 0.8], fs=8.5)
P("Note: the workbook’s “Notes” column does not flag Thornwall as undisclosed, and its summary row states only “5” undisclosed matters involving either firm. Both are wrong: Thornwall does not appear in the disclosure, and the correct count is seven completed matters plus Halcyon (eight in total).", italic=True)
P("**Effect of the omissions on the picture presented.** The disclosed record presents this firm as 3–0 in completed matters (NorthPoint, Meridian, Braddock) with one pending (Orion), and Fielding Marsh as 1–1 with one settlement. The full record is this firm **8–1** across nine completed matters and Fielding Marsh **1–3** across four adjudicated matters (plus one settlement). The omitted Westbrook matter is the only prior contest between the two firms before this arbitrator — and Fielding Marsh lost. Because the disclosure volunteered outcomes “solely for purposes of transparency,” a selective list that understates one counsel’s success rate is likely to be characterized as misleading, not merely incomplete.", align="j")
P("**Assessment.** This is the strongest ground. R-17(a)(iii) is categorical (“any prior or pending cases”), these matters are within the arbitrator’s own records (so “known” cannot credibly be disputed), and the omission of a pending matter accepted only seven weeks before this appointment cannot be explained by faulty recollection. Under R-18(d) the AAA weighs “disclosures required but not made.” IBA Orange List 3.3.8 (more than three appointments involving the same firm within three years) is satisfied many times over. Halliburton v. Chubb (persuasive) treats undisclosed overlapping appointments involving a common party as a breach of the duty of disclosure. **Who raises it:** Cascade. **Strength:** High. The omission of Westbrook and Thornwall (Fielding Marsh losses) also undermines any argument that the omissions were neutral.", align="j")

H("2. Economic Dependence and Repeat-Player Concerns", 2)
P("**Corrected figures (workbook Case List, 20 completed matters):**", align="j")
T(["Metric", "Workbook / June 19 memo", "Corrected (recomputed from Case List rows)"], [
 ["Total fees, 20 completed matters", "$2,125,000", "$1,974,000 (sum of the 20 rows); the $151,000 difference is unexplained"],
 ["B&T matters / fees", "9 / $1,020,000", "9 / $1,020,000 (confirmed)"],
 ["B&T share of income", "48.0%", "51.7% ($1,020,000 ÷ $1,974,000)"],
 ["B&T client prevailed", "7 of 9 (77.8%)", "8 of 9 (88.9%) — only Trident Coatings was lost"],
 ["FM matters / fees", "Workbook: 5 / $410,000; June 19 memo: 4 / $280,000", "5 / $410,000 (memo omitted Westbrook); 20.8% of income"],
 ["FM client prevailed", "1 of 4 (25.0%)", "1 of 4 adjudicated (25.0%) (confirmed) + 1 settled"],
 ["Pending fees involving B&T", "$560,000 of $835,000 (67.1%)", "Confirmed: this matter $340,000 + Orion $45,000 + Halcyon $175,000"],
 ["Completed + pending, B&T share", "—", "$1,580,000 of $2,809,000 (56.2%); excluding this matter, $1,240,000 of $2,469,000 (50.2%)"],
], widths=[1.8, 2.0, 2.7], fs=8.5)
P("**Analysis.** On any computation, roughly half of the arbitrator’s documented fee income over the period derives from matters in which this firm appeared, she has three concurrent matters involving this firm (including one where an award is expected within 60 days), and our clients have prevailed in nearly nine of ten. Win-rate statistics do not themselves establish bias (outcomes reflect the merits and small samples), and the workbook covers only 20 of roughly 85 arbitrations, so the true share of her total income may be lower. But the R-16 standard is whether a reasonable person would consider the circumstance relevant, and an income concentration of this magnitude, undisclosed, is the type of economic relationship that Commonwealth Coatings and Monster Energy treat as material. The fees are paid by the parties, not counsel, but the repeat-appointment relationship is with counsel. **Who raises it:** Cascade. **Strength:** High when combined with Issue 1. Caveat: the fee figures are estimates compiled from public data; any filing should describe them as such.", align="j")
P("**Pending-matter timing.** The disclosure says she expects to issue the Orion award within 60 days, i.e., during this case’s pre-hearing phase. Any award or new appointment involving this firm during the pendency of this matter is a continuing-disclosure event under R-17(b) and should be expressly requested.", align="j")

H("3. Garrett T. Whitmore — Board of Trustees, Minnesota ADR Ethics Institute", 2)
P("**What the disclosure says.** Section VI discloses her advisory board service (since 2021) and Ellen Wu’s, describes the board as meeting twice yearly in a voluntary, non-binding capacity, and states she is “not aware of any other organizational affiliation that would give rise to justifiable doubt.” Section I states she reviewed “the individuals identified in the arbitration demand” — which names Mr. Whitmore as Respondent’s Managing Partner and an adverse witness.", align="j")
P("**What the record shows.** The Institute’s FY2023 Form 990 lists Mr. Whitmore as a Trustee. The Board of Trustees is the governing body; it is responsible for leadership appointments, advisory board members are appointed by or serve at the pleasure of the Trustees, and the Institute holds annual meetings and joint Trustee/advisory board sessions. The Institute is a small organization.", align="j")
P("**Assessment.** R-17(a)(ii) expressly identifies “board memberships” and “professional association” with a party or witness. This is a relationship with the respondent’s principal (not merely counsel, so IBA Green List 4.3.1 does not apply), the governing body on which he sits controls her seat, and he will be an adverse witness whose credibility she must assess on the central “who directed the deal” issue. Given the small size of the body and joint sessions, it is unlikely she was unaware of his role. **Who raises it:** Cascade. **Strength:** High, and it compounds Issue 8 (Ms. Wu sits on the same advisory board and was involved in selection strategy). Whitmore’s own knowledge of this fact is obvious, which heightens the concealment optics if it is not surfaced now.", align="j")

H("4. Indirect Financial Interest — Northbridge Select Alternatives Fund / Whitmore Fund II LP", 2)
P("**What the disclosure says.** Section IV: her portfolio is managed on a discretionary basis by Northbridge Wealth Advisors; she holds “no direct equity positions in any party”; she has “not undertaken a position-by-position review” of pooled vehicles or fund-of-funds structures; and she is “not aware” of any material indirect interest.", align="j")
P("**What the record shows.** Northbridge manages the Northbridge Select Alternatives Fund, which (per a March 2024 filing) holds a 2.3% LP interest in Whitmore Fund II LP — the Respondent-managed fund that owns Volaris, the beneficiary of the challenged license. Whether her account holds the Northbridge fund is unconfirmed.", align="j")
P("**Assessment.** R-17(a)(i) reaches “direct or indirect” interests in “any entity that may be affected by the result.” Fund II is a privately held affiliate of the Respondent (IBA Waivable Red List 2.2.1 covers indirect holdings in a privately held affiliate). The economic direction matters: rescission, repricing, or disgorgement against Volaris would reduce Fund II’s value, so any such interest aligns with Respondent. The disclosure is carefully drafted (“no direct equity positions”) and concedes she did not check — which is itself a failure of the Canon II.B/IBA GS 7(d) duty of reasonable inquiry, particularly once she read a Demand describing Fund II and Volaris. The interest, if held, may be economically trivial (her share of a 2.3% LP stake), and Positive Software warns against vacatur for trivial, remote interests; but its existence would be a strong removal ground at the challenge stage where doubts are resolved in favor of disclosure. **Who raises it:** Cascade. **Strength:** High if confirmed; Moderate on the inquiry failure alone. Note that Whitmore, as GP, knows the identity of Fund II’s LPs, including Northbridge Select.", align="j")

H("5. Spouse’s Co-Authorship with Dr. Rita Peshkov (Claimant’s Key Technical Expert)", 2)
P("**What the disclosure says.** Section V: Dr. Alan Fairhaven retired from teaching in 2019, holds emeritus status, “does not currently serve in any consulting or advisory capacity to any party,” “is not currently engaged in any active research collaborations with industrial partners,” and, to her knowledge, has “no financial or professional relationship with Cascade … or any of their officers, directors, or employees.”", align="j")
P("**What the record shows.** Dr. Alan Fairhaven and Dr. Rita Peshkov co-authored “Optimization of Phase-Change Heat Exchangers in High-Load Industrial Applications,” Journal of Advanced Thermal Engineering, Vol. 42, Issue 3 (September 2022) — three years after his retirement from teaching. Dr. Peshkov is a Cascade employee (VP R&D since 2017), the named inventor on most ThermalCore patents, and Claimant’s “key expert witness”; the paper’s subject (phase-change heat exchangers for high-load industrial use) is the ThermalCore technology class.", align="j")
P("**Assessment.** R-17(a)(ii) expressly covers past “professional, family” relationships with “witnesses,” and lists “academic collaboration.” The Code of Ethics extends disclosure to family members’ relationships. The disclosure’s qualifiers (“currently,” “any party”) do not cure the omission, and its statement that her husband has no professional relationship with Cascade’s employees appears inaccurate as to a past relationship. The concern is concrete: the arbitrator will assess Dr. Peshkov’s credibility and the uniqueness/value of the technology, which drives the $9.5M FMV and the $46.9M claim; she may also be exposed to her husband’s views on the technology. Mitigating factors: one paper, two years old, no evidence of current collaboration or financial ties; it is the spouse’s, not the arbitrator’s, relationship. **Who raises it:** Whitmore. **Strength:** Moderate–High; stronger if inquiry shows continuing collaboration, joint grants, or any consulting with Cascade. **Waiver:** this is the one ground Whitmore loses by silence (R-18(a)(ii), (f)), because it is now known to us (June 19 memo).", align="j")

H("6. CLE Co-Panel with Dominic Hargrave (October 14, 2023)", 2)
P("**What the record shows.** Judge Fairhaven and you were co-panelists on “Arbitrating Complex IP Licensing Disputes,” hosted by Lakeview at its offices, five months before the Demand. Topics included valuation methodologies, arbitrator selection in technology-intensive cases, and management of expert testimony — all live issues here (Ridgeline’s methodology; Dr. Peshkov’s expert role). Not disclosed.", align="j")
P("**Assessment.** Standing alone, joint conference speaking with counsel is ordinarily non-disqualifying (IBA Green List 4.3.4), so this is not an independent removal ground. But under the broader AAA standard it is a “professional” relationship with lead counsel under R-17(a)(ii) and potentially “expressed views on legal or factual issues relevant to the dispute” under R-17(a)(iv), and it occurred at the institution with which she is affiliated and which receives referrals from this firm. In combination with Issues 1–3, it supports a narrative of a close professional relationship with Respondent’s side. Its omission is hard to explain: she was on the panel, and the Demand names you. **Who raises it:** Cascade. **Strength:** Moderate as an aggravating factor. **Action:** please confirm the nature of your preparation/interaction for the panel, any subsequent contact, and whether any recording or materials exist that reflect her views on valuation or expert evidence.", align="j")

H("7. Lakeview Dispute Resolution Center Affiliation", 2)
P("**What the disclosure says.** Section VII discloses the affiliation and that Lakeview receives referrals from both firms, characterizes this as typical, and notes Lakeview has no role in this AAA case.", align="j")
P("**What is missing.** The structure of her relationship (employee, independent contractor, member/owner), whether she shares in Lakeview revenues or administrative fees, and the volume and value of referrals from each firm. Lakeview also hosted the undisclosed CLE with you.", align="j")
P("**Assessment.** Monster Energy vacated an award where the arbitrator did not disclose an ownership interest in the provider and the provider’s repeat business with a party; if she has an equity or revenue interest in Lakeview and this firm is a material referral source, the same logic applies to counsel. The disclosure’s reassurance that referrals do not influence her is not a substitute for the facts. **Who raises it:** Either party (both firms refer). **Strength:** Moderate pending the facts; potentially High if she has an ownership interest and referrals from this firm are significant.", align="j")

H("8. Ellen Wu — Shared Advisory Board Service", 2)
P("The disclosure accurately discloses Ms. Wu’s advisory board service since 2021, and alone this is a Green List-type association. Two qualifications: (i) the disclosure describes the board’s role as “non-binding guidance,” while the Institute materials describe “substantive guidance on programming, ethics standards, and professional development”; and (ii) Ms. Wu heads this firm’s arbitration practice and was involved in arbitrator selection strategy for this case, which Cascade may characterize as Respondent choosing a familiar colleague. Combined with Issue 3 (Mr. Whitmore on the governing board of the same small organization), the Institute connection links the arbitrator to Respondent’s principal and Respondent’s practice head. **Strength:** Low alone; aggravating in combination.", align="j")

H("9. Subject-Matter Experience and Possible Issue Conflicts", 2)
P("Section VIII states she has presided over “numerous” arbitrations involving technology licensing, IP valuation, and “fiduciary duty claims in the context of private equity portfolio management,” including “the standards of care applicable to investment fund managers in connection with portfolio company transactions.” Expertise is not a conflict, but (i) the statement implies prior rulings on the same legal issues, potentially in matters involving these counsel (e.g., Braddock v. Summit Ridge Capital, an earn-out dispute in which she was this firm’s party-appointed arbitrator; Westbrook Partners v. Arcadian Ventures), which would bear on IBA Orange List 3.1.5 and R-17(a)(iv); and (ii) the CLE and any publications may reflect views on reasonable-royalty and valuation methods. We should request identification (anonymized if confidential) of prior matters addressing PE fund manager duties in cross-fund or affiliate transactions, and any publications or public statements on those issues. **Strength:** Low–Moderate pending responses.", align="j")

H("10. Certification, Timing and Other Defects", 2)
B("**Certification.** Section X certifies completeness “based on a diligent inquiry” while Section IV concedes no position-level review. The certification is contradicted by the record on at least the case list, which is within her own knowledge. R-17(d) makes incomplete disclosure a removal and vacatur ground, and the AAA will view the inaccuracy as aggravating.")
B("**Narrow drafting.** Repeated limiting language — “direct” equity (IV), “currently” and “any party” (V), “socialized with … counsel” (V), “to the best of my recollection” (III) — tracks almost exactly the relationships that were omitted. This pattern will be emphasized by any challenger.")
B("**Confidential-name entry.** Item 3 (Fielding Marsh settled matter, 2021) withholds names; withholding is acceptable but the case number, her role, and counsel on the other side should be provided (the workbook lists the opposing counsel as “Undisclosed”).")
B("**Timing.** R-12(a) contemplates that disclosures accompany the list; here disclosure followed selection (June 3) and confirmation (June 10). Not itself a ground, but it means the parties ranked her without the facts.")
B("**Deadline statement.** The disclosure states the objection period runs seven days from the disclosure (June 24). Under R-18(a) the period runs from the later of communication of the appointment or knowledge of the circumstances. For Whitmore, the facts in the June 19 memo are known now; we should treat June 24 as the outside date for every ground Whitmore might raise. For Cascade, the clock on undisclosed facts will not start until it learns them.")
B("**Items checked and found accurate.** Fee math (400 hours × $850 = $340,000; 15 days × 8 hours = 120 hearing hours; $170,000 per party); hearing window January 13 – February 7, 2025 accommodates 15 hearing days; disclosed matter details (roles, outcomes, counsel) for the seven listed matters are consistent with the workbook; Orion was appointed September 15, 2023 with $45,000 remaining fees.")
EOF

S=/home/user/Lawless_Research_Lab/harvey_lab/sbx.sh; R=/home/user/Lawless_Research_Lab/harvey_lab/vendor/harvey-labs/results/arbitration-international-dispute-resolution/identify-issues-in-arbitrator-disclosure-statement/claude-code-session/20261016-031557; $S $R 'cat > /workspace/build4.py <<"EOF"
H("V. Cumulative Assessment")
P("**A challenge by Cascade.** The AAA decides challenges on the totality of circumstances, including “disclosures required but not made” (R-18(d)). Even if some items (CLE, Ms. Wu) would be tolerated alone, the combination — eight omitted matters, a ~52% income concentration with Respondent’s counsel, three concurrent matters with this firm, an undisclosed governance link to Respondent’s principal, a possible indirect stake in the Respondent fund that owns the license beneficiary, a germane CLE with Respondent’s lead counsel, and an inaccurate certification — would in our judgment very likely lead the AAA to sustain a challenge, or lead the arbitrator to withdraw. R-18(f) would not bar Cascade, because these facts were not disclosed and, except arguably through public-record research, could not reasonably have been known. We should not rely on a constructive-knowledge waiver argument: the AAA text excuses grounds that “could not reasonably have been known,” and arguing that Cascade should have unearthed what the arbitrator certified did not exist would be unattractive.", align="j")
P("**Vacatur exposure.** If the case proceeds to a Respondent award and Cascade later learns the facts, it would move to vacate under FAA § 10(a)(2) (and R-17(d)). Courts set a high bar for evident partiality and reject trivial undisclosed relationships (Positive Software), but nondisclosure of significant, known economic relationships with a side is the core Commonwealth Coatings scenario, and Monster Energy is a close analog on institution/repeat-business facts. A vacatur after a 15-day hearing and roughly $340,000 in arbitrator fees alone (plus both sides’ costs) would be the worst outcome for Whitmore: it would lose a defense win on a $46.9M+ claim and face a re-hearing before a new arbitrator, with the concealment narrative attached. The fact that this firm compiled the facts on June 19 from public sources, and that our client and this firm independently knew most of them, would feature prominently.", align="j")
P("**A challenge by Whitmore.** Whitmore’s only Claimant-side ground is the spouse–Peshkov co-authorship (Issue 5), plus Lakeview referrals from Fielding Marsh (Issue 7, weak). On its own it is a credible but not certain ground. A Whitmore challenge would also inevitably prompt a supplemental disclosure that surfaces Issues 1–4 and 6, so it should be considered together with the disclosure-request strategy below.", align="j")
P("**Professional-responsibility overlay.** Counsel generally has no affirmative obligation to supplement an arbitrator’s disclosure, but this firm is not a stranger to the omitted facts (its own cases, its lead partner’s CLE, its practice head’s board service, its client’s trustee role and LP register). Remaining silent while relying on the arbitrator’s certification invites a later argument that Respondent waived nothing because it knew everything, while Cascade waived nothing because it knew nothing — the asymmetric posture that maximizes vacatur risk. We also must avoid any ex parte communication with the arbitrator on these subjects (R-20). The applicable Minnesota and Massachusetts rules of professional conduct (candor and conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice) should be reviewed by the firm’s General Counsel before any decision to remain silent.", align="j")

H("VI. Strategic Options")
T(["Option", "Description", "Advantages", "Risks", "View"], [
 ["A. Remain silent", "File nothing by June 24; proceed with a favorable arbitrator.", "Keeps Whitmore’s first-choice arbitrator.", "Waives Whitmore’s Peshkov ground; leaves Cascade free to challenge later or seek vacatur of any Respondent award; concealment optics for client and firm.", "Not recommended"],
 ["B. Request supplemental disclosure + protective reservation (recommended)", "Letter to AAA (copy to FM) under R-17(b)–(d) listing the specific subjects in Section VIII; expressly reserve/assert Whitmore’s objection on the spouse–Peshkov ground and request that the objection period run from the supplemental disclosure.", "Cures nondisclosure; starts Cascade’s 7-day clock (R-18(a), (f)), insulating any award; preserves Whitmore’s ground; demonstrates good faith.", "Cascade may challenge and the arbitrator may be removed or withdraw (early replacement is far cheaper than vacatur); the AAA may treat a reservation as insufficient — hence also include a specific written challenge in the alternative.", "Recommended"],
 ["C. Formal challenge by Whitmore on Peshkov ground only", "R-18 challenge stating grounds with specificity, without broader disclosure request.", "Preserves Whitmore’s ground.", "Supplemental disclosure will follow anyway; selectively raising only the Claimant-side ground while silent on Respondent-side facts known to us would look tactical and would not cure vacatur risk.", "Not recommended standing alone"],
 ["D. Agree to replacement now", "Propose jointly with Cascade a replacement under R-19 / R-12.", "Clean record; minimal cost at this stage (preliminary hearing not until Aug. 5, 2024).", "Loses Whitmore’s preferred arbitrator; requires client consent.", "Fallback if supplemental disclosure confirms Northbridge holding or Lakeview equity"],
], widths=[1.1, 1.6, 1.3, 1.6, 0.9], fs=8.5)

H("VII. Recommended Action Plan")
T(["Date", "Action", "Owner"], [
 ["June 20 (today)", "Brief Whitmore (Garrett T. Whitmore and in-house counsel) on this memo; obtain instructions. Confirm Mr. Whitmore’s trustee role, his interactions with the arbitrator at Institute meetings, and whether Northbridge Select appears on Fund II’s LP register (and the size/timing of its commitment).", "D. Hargrave"],
 ["June 20–21", "Confirm internally (conflicts/records) the B&T matters before Judge Fairhaven (incl. Halcyon and the six omitted completed matters) and the fee estimates; confirm your CLE interactions. Have firm General Counsel review the professional-responsibility questions. Wall off Ellen Wu from the decision.", "Case team; GC"],
 ["June 20–21", "Verify rule text against the official AAA Commercial Rules and update the case law cited in Section III.C (Eighth Circuit evident-partiality standard; Minn. Stat. ch. 572B).", "Associate"],
 ["By Fri. June 21 (no later than Mon. June 24)", "Serve on the AAA, with simultaneous copy to Fielding Marsh (R-18(a), R-20, R-48 — email plus overnight), a letter (i) requesting supplemental disclosure on the Section VIII topics; (ii) asserting Whitmore’s objection on the spouse–Peshkov ground with specificity, in the alternative as an R-18 challenge, and reserving the right to supplement within seven days of the supplemental disclosure; (iii) requesting that the AAA treat the objection period as running from the supplemental disclosure.", "D. Hargrave"],
 ["Upon supplemental disclosure", "Reassess within 7 days; decide whether to maintain, withdraw, or expand the challenge; prepare response to any Cascade challenge (R-18(b): 7 days).", "Case team"],
 ["Ongoing", "Calendar continuing-disclosure triggers: Orion award (expected within ~60 days), any new appointment involving this firm, Halcyon developments. Do not communicate with the arbitrator ex parte.", "Case team"],
], widths=[1.3, 4.2, 1.0], fs=8.5)

H("VIII. Proposed Topics for Supplemental Disclosure")
N("All prior and pending matters (any institution or ad hoc) since 2020 in which Barrow & Thistlewood LLP or Fielding Marsh & Collier LLP appeared, with case number, her role, the appointing method, counsel on each side, outcome, and the status of Orion and Halcyon Biotech; confirmation of any new appointments since June 17, 2024.")
N("Approximate share of her arbitration and mediation income attributable to matters involving each firm over the past three years.")
N("Whether she, her spouse, or any household member holds, directly or through any managed account, pooled vehicle, or fund-of-funds (including the Northbridge Select Alternatives Fund), any interest in Whitmore Capital Partners LLC, Whitmore Fund I, II or III LP, Volaris, Cascade, or any Whitmore portfolio company; and a request that she obtain a position-level confirmation from Northbridge Wealth Advisors.")
N("Her relationship with Garrett T. Whitmore, including through the Minnesota ADR Ethics Institute (Board of Trustees/advisory board structure, appointment of advisory board members, joint sessions, and any personal interaction), and with Ellen Wu.")
N("Any professional, academic, or personal relationship between Dr. Alan Fairhaven and Dr. Rita Peshkov or any other Cascade or Volaris personnel, including the September 2022 co-authored article, related research, grants, consulting, or ongoing contact; and any work by Dr. Fairhaven relating to phase-change heat-exchange technology or ThermalCore.")
N("All speaking engagements, CLE panels, publications, or public statements since 2020 with counsel of record or addressing IP licensing valuation, reasonable royalties, expert evidence, or PE fund-manager duties in affiliate transactions — including the October 14, 2023 Lakeview CLE.")
N("The structure and economics of her Lakeview affiliation (employment/contractor/ownership; revenue or fee sharing) and the approximate volume of referrals to Lakeview from each firm.")
N("Prior matters (anonymized if necessary) in which she decided fiduciary-duty claims against PE fund managers arising from cross-fund or affiliate transactions.")

H("Appendix A — Reconciliation of All Matters Involving Either Firm")
T(["Case No.", "Matter", "Year", "B&T role", "FM role", "Arbitrator role", "Prevailing", "Disclosed?"], [
 ["01-21-0001482", "NorthPoint Logistics v. Grainger Holdings", "2021", "Resp.", "—", "Sole", "B&T client", "Yes (#1)"],
 ["01-21-0001637", "[Confidential] (lease)", "2021", "—", "Claimant", "Sole", "Settled", "Yes (#3)"],
 ["01-22-0001894", "Meridian Software v. TelBridge", "2022", "Claimant", "—", "Chair", "B&T client", "Yes (#2)"],
